sources.title: Logan, Lively & Pisoni (1991): Training Japanese listeners to identify English /r/ and /l/: A first report
sources.locator: Methods B–C; Discussion; DOI 10.1121/1.1894649
sources.whatItSupports: Japanese adults; natural /r–l/ words, varied speakers and phonetic environments; held-out words and speaker tests.
sources.limitations: Identification training with visible alternatives, not this product’s cross-word audio-only ABX. Small initial study. Full stimulus table not recovered in this pass.
sources.license: Article copyright ASA; no recording-reuse permission inferred.

sources.title: Lively, Logan & Pisoni (1993): Training Japanese listeners to identify English /r/ and /l/. II
sources.locator: Experiments 1–2; DOI 10.1121/1.408177
sources.whatItSupports: Explicit investigation of talker and phonetic-environment variability for Japanese /r–l/ learning.
sources.limitations: Study-specific identification results do not establish an optimal number of voices or ABX superiority.

sources.title: Iverson, Hazan & Bannister (2005): Phonetic training with acoustic cue manipulations
sources.locator: JASA 118(5), 3267–3278; natural recordings and Appendix Table A1
sources.whatItSupports: Japanese adults trained on initial /r–l/ words; additional medial and cluster tests.
sources.limitations: British recordings; our American IPA is an editorial adaptation. Natural and manipulated identification conditions were compared; no blanket claim of superiority for manipulations.

sources.title: Iverson et al. (2005), Appendix Table A1: Words used in the experiment
sources.locator: Published paper p.3276, Table A1; full-text appendix inspected at this mirror
sources.whatItSupports: Exact lexical membership of the selected /r–l/ words marked stimulusSourceIds, including training, new-initial, medial and cluster sections.
sources.limitations: Membership only: not our American IPA, meanings, audio or training/test split. This inventory deliberately mixes original experimental roles and must create a new held-out split. Publisher DOI is the bibliographic authority.
sources.license: ASA copyright; no audio/images copied or reuse license inferred.

sources.title: Shinohara & Iverson (2018): High variability identification and discrimination training for Japanese speakers learning English /r–l/
sources.locator: Sections 2.2–2.4 and Discussion; DOI 10.1016/j.wocn.2017.11.002
sources.whatItSupports: Both identification and mixed discrimination training improved Japanese learners’ English /r–l/.
sources.limitations: The discrimination program mixed three tasks, including cross-word oddity. Speakers varied across sessions. Identification had a larger early identification-test gain. This was not our ABX algorithm.
sources.license: CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 article; no commercial asset reuse inferred.

sources.title: Giannakopoulou, Brown, Clayards & Wonnacott (2017): High or low? Comparing high and low-variability phonetic training in adult and child second language learners
sources.locator: Stimuli and Training; Abstract; PeerJ 5:e3209
sources.whatItSupports: Greek children/adults trained on /i–ɪ/ with 20 real minimal pairs and tested with real and novel nonwords; five Southern British speakers recorded stimuli.
sources.limitations: Training used picture identification; no general high-variability advantage was established. Table S1 retrieval failed, so none of our words receives stimulus-list provenance from this paper.
sources.license: CC BY article; supplement/audio license not independently inspected.

sources.title: Nishi & Kewley-Port (2008): Non-native speech perception training using vowel subsets: Effects of vowels in sets and order of training
sources.locator: Abstract and study description; PubMed https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18664694/
sources.whatItSupports: Korean learners trained on nine American vowel categories; situates earlier Japanese nine-vowel training. Supports broader vowel-category coverage.
sources.limitations: Accessible indexed abstract/study description only in this pass; PMC body returned a browser challenge. Does not validate every binary contrast, word pool or task proposed here.

sources.title: Lambacher et al. (2001): Identification of English voiceless fricatives by Japanese listeners: The influence of vowel context on sensitivity and response bias
sources.locator: Methods 2.1–2.2; Table 1; Discussion, pp.334–343
sources.whatItSupports: 104 Japanese listeners identified /f,s,ʃ,θ,h/ in varied syllable/vowel contexts. Confusions motivate /θ–s/, /ʃ–s/ and /f–h/.
sources.limitations: Perception study, not an intervention trial. Stimuli were nonsense syllables; our real words are editorial. Vowel context materially changes difficulty, especially /ʃ–s/ near /i/ and /f–h/ near /u/.

sources.title: Leong et al. (2018): High variability phonetic training in adaptive adverse conditions is rapid, effective, and sustained
sources.locator: Experiment 1 Design and stimuli/Procedure; Experiments 2–3; DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0204888
sources.whatItSupports: Malaysian multilingual participants; /ɛ–æ/ training and tests including final /t–d/. Varied talkers and held-out items were considered.
sources.limitations: Training was same–different in babble; final /t–d/ was an untrained generalization contrast. Initial /t–d/ was near ceiling. No imported word list and no noise-training requirement inferred.
sources.license: CC BY article; no audio files copied.

sources.title: Inceoglu (2016), Effects of perceptual training on second language vowel perception and production

sources.limitations: Author abstract and later author discussion checked; full stimulus appendix not recovered. No words are attributed to this experiment.

sources.title: Inceoglu (2022), A web-based high variability phonetic training application for French vowels
sources.locator: Table 1, printed p.4; pp.5–6
sources.whatItSupports: Explicit familiarization words for the Ouïe application, tagged individually below.
sources.limitations: Application-development paper, not a controlled efficacy trial. Familiarization examples are not its complete 181-word training inventory. Training uses phoneme identification with IPA choices. Full-word IPA/glosses here are editorial.

sources.title: Kingston (2003), Learning Foreign Vowels
sources.locator: Methods pp.305–307; Table 1
sources.whatItSupports: American-English learners, 12 German nonlow vowel categories, identification training with five speakers and varied consonantal frames.
sources.limitations: Words and pseudowords in stressed CVCn frames. No full lexical bank recovered. Inventory coverage does not prove every selected binary contrast below was separately trained.

sources.title: Gao et al. (2019), Perception of German tense and lax vowel contrast by Chinese learners

sources.whatItSupports: Seven tense/lax vowel pairs; Mandarin-Chinese listeners and German controls; quality/duration manipulations.
sources.limitations: Perception experiment with synthesized words, not HVPT. Full 70-word list not recovered; no word below is claimed as its stimulus.

sources.locator: Consonants, vowels, stress; DOI 10.1017/S0025100316000232
sources.whatItSupports: Mexican Spanish inventory and contextual variation.
sources.limitations: Descriptive phonology; neither a training trial nor verification of every proposed lemma.

sources.title: Herd, Jongman & Sereno: Perceptual and production training of intervocalic /d, ɾ, r/ in American English learners of Spanish
sources.locator: Methods pp.4248–4250; six training sessions; Table I summarizes allocation
sources.whatItSupports: Direct L2 training of three intervocalic contrasts; generalization measures.
sources.limitations: Identification used written choices. Does not validate text-free cross-word ABX. Published article does not provide the full lexical table; candidate words are not labeled table-confirmed stimuli.

sources.title: Bertinetto & Loporcaro: The sound pattern of Standard Italian, as compared with Florence, Milan and Rome
sources.locator: Consonantal length pp.3–5; vowel inventory and regional distribution pp.6–9
sources.whatItSupports: Standard Italian length and stressed mid-vowel contrasts.
sources.limitations: Regional lexical distributions differ. Predictable vowel duration is not an independent vowel-length contrast.

sources.title: De Iacovo et al.: The perception of gemination in Italian by first-language speakers in Italy and heritage and second-language speakers in Australia
sources.locator: Methods §2.1, PDF p.6; named /p,t,k/ word pairs; Table 1 durations
sources.whatItSupports: L2 singleton/geminate perception; explicitly names papa/pappa, fata/fatta, paca/pacca.
sources.limitations: Synthetic and duration-manipulated identification experiment; not a training intervention. Named words occur in methods prose, not a lexical table; stimulusSourceIds deliberately empty under table-only policy.

sources.title: Dong, Clayards, Brown & Wonnacott: The effects of high versus low talker variability and individual aptitude on phonetic training of Mandarin lexical tones
sources.locator: Methods, Stimuli; Conclusion; Appendix A link
sources.whatItSupports: All six pairwise tone contrasts in 36 real-word pairs; transfer tests.
sources.limitations: Mostly English-L1 adults without prior tone-language learning. No overall high-variability generalization advantage. Appendix located but download failed, so no proposed word receives this as stimulusSourceIds.

sources.title: Dong et al. Appendix A: Thirty-six pairs of Mandarin words
sources.locator: Supplement 1, 16.2 KB DOCX
sources.whatItSupports: A real-word stimulus list exists and is a priority for exact extraction.
sources.limitations: Not retrieved: publisher 403; PMC attachment returned non-DOCX. Not evidence that any particular candidate word appeared.

sources.title: Lee & Zee: Standard Chinese (Beijing)
sources.locator: JIPA 33(1), 109–112; publisher record
sources.whatItSupports: Reference for target-variety inventory.
sources.limitations: Publisher HTML record accessed; full phonetic illustration not extracted. New consonant pools remain editorial candidates pending complete source and lexical checks.

sources.title: Open University: Mandarin tones
sources.locator: Four citation tones
sources.whatItSupports: Pedagogical citation-tone categories.
sources.limitations: Not L2 efficacy evidence; running-speech realizations differ.

sources.title: Smirnova Henriques et al.: The perception of Brazilian Portuguese open and close mid vowels by native Russian speakers
sources.locator: Tables 4–6, PDF pp.13–14
sources.whatItSupports: Table-confirmed real words for stressed e/ɛ and o/ɔ; Russian-L1 perception difficulty.
sources.limitations: Perception assessment, not training efficacy. Loanword and nonminimal contexts were not imported. Full IPA below is editorial normalization; tables mark target vowels.

sources.title: Martinez, Goad & Dow: L1 phonological effects on L2 (non-)naïve perception: a cross-language investigation of the oral–nasal vowel contrast in Brazilian Portuguese
sources.locator: Stimuli and methods
sources.whatItSupports: L1-dependent oral–nasal perception across French, English and Spanish varieties.
sources.limitations: Artificial monosyllables: not evidence for real-word pools or the proposed low-vowel pair.

sources.title: Similar, Yet Different: Acquisition of Brazilian Portuguese Nasal Vowels by Spanish-English Bilinguals
sources.whatItSupports: Table-confirmed oral and nasal Portuguese words, including fado and santo.
sources.limitations: Small L3 production study (four learners); not perceptual training or proof of a minimal pair. Full IPA is normalized here; contexts differ.

sources.title: Barbosa & Albano: Brazilian Portuguese
sources.locator: JIPA 34(2),227–232; publisher record
sources.whatItSupports: Reference target variety for existing Brazilian Portuguese pools.
sources.limitations: Full text not extracted here; new rhotic candidates require a chosen regional realization.

sources.title: Simonchyk & Darcy: The Effect of Orthography on the Lexical Encoding of Palatalized Consonants in L2 Russian
sources.locator: Public Appendix table: target words, test nonwords and control nonwords
sources.whatItSupports: Real-word target columns and position-specific palatalization study in American English learners.
sources.limitations: Assessment, not training efficacy. Nonword columns excluded. IPA normalized rather than copied mechanically; word pools are not minimal pairs.

sources.title: Yanushevskaya & Bunčić: Russian
sources.locator: JIPA 45(2),221–228; indexed consonant discussion
sources.whatItSupports: Plain/palatalized consonants and inventory context.
sources.limitations: Full publisher page unavailable in this pass; indexed primary text supports broad categories. Lexical additions need entry checks.

sources.title: Russian Academy of Sciences: Orthographic commentary of the Russian dictionary
sources.locator: Hardness/softness examples; Russian orthographic dictionary basis
sources.whatItSupports: Explicit лук/люк and нос/нёс category examples.
sources.limitations: Orthographic resource, not a perceptual training trial or detailed phonetic transcription.

sources.title: Tsukada, Cox, Hajek & Hirata (2018): Non-native Japanese learners’ perception of consonant length in Japanese and Italian
sources.locator: Publisher abstract; first online 2017, volume 34(2), 2018
sources.whatItSupports: Australian English and Korean learners of Japanese also performed Italian consonant-length identification; linguistic experience affected error direction. Supports attention to L1 experience in length contrasts.
sources.limitations: Abstract inspected; no word table recovered. This is identification/perception evidence, not a demonstration that this product’s cross-word ABX training is superior. No new words receive stimulus provenance from it.

sources.title: Martinez, Goad & Dow (2023): L1 phonological effects on L2 (non-)naïve perception
sources.locator: Publisher abstract; first online 2021, volume 39(2), 2023
sources.whatItSupports: AXB perception of Brazilian Portuguese /e–ẽ/ and /i–ĩ/ depended on French, English and Spanish listener background and prior exposure. Identifies remaining nasal-vowel priorities beyond the current low-vowel draft.
sources.limitations: These were controlled syllable contrasts, not our newly curated whole words or a low-vowel training efficacy trial. No study-word links assigned from the abstract.

sources.title: Dong, Clayards, Brown & Wonnacott: The effects of high versus low talker variability and individual aptitude on phonetic training of Mandarin lexical tones
sources.locator: Methods, Stimuli; Conclusion; Appendix A link
sources.whatItSupports: All six pairwise tone contrasts in 36 real-word pairs; transfer tests.

sources.title: Lan Yu: Perception of Mandarin Sibilant Fricatives by American English learners
sources.locator: Publisher abstract; volume 16(1), issue labelled 2016, online publication 2018
sources.whatItSupports: American English learners were tested on Mandarin sibilant identification; experience and linguistic context affected identification.
sources.limitations: Abstract read, not the complete stimulus table. Supports the relevance of sibilant/context work, not a ranking or validation of this exact new pool. No study words or audio imported.

sources.title: Wang & Chen (2020): The Acquisition of Mandarin Consonants by English Learners: The Relationship between Perception and Production
sources.locator: Indexed primary abstract and results discussion; 25 English CFL learners
sources.whatItSupports: Retroflex, palatal and dental fricatives/affricates create different perception and production problems in this learner sample.
sources.limitations: Primary indexed text read; direct page returned 429. Does not establish a universal L1 ranking or an advantage for product cross-word ABX.

sources.title: Wang, Cui & Chen (2018): Wuxi Speakers’ Production and Perception of Coda Nasals in Mandarin
sources.locator: ISCA publisher abstract, two perception/production experiments
sources.whatItSupports: Wuxi Wu speakers learning Mandarin were tested on alveolar/velar nasal codas; age groups differed in production and identification.
sources.limitations: Specific Wu-background population. This is not a training trial and does not establish universal n/ng difficulty. No stimulus table or recordings imported.

sources.title: Collins Italian–English Dictionary: zuppa
sources.locator: Italian headword pronunciation [ˈtsuppa] and noun sense soup; entry directly read in independent audit 2026-10-01.
sources.whatItSupports: The selected standard reading begins with voiceless /ts/ and contains geminate /p/. The displayed [ˈtsuppa] is normalized to broad /ˈtsupːa/ by writing pp as pː; supports the soup sense.
sources.limitations: Dictionary transcription and sense verified, not an auditioned recording. Broad length notation is an explicit editorial normalization. This is dictionary-curated vocabulary, not recovered study stimuli.

sources.title: Dizionario italiano Olivetti: zuppa
sources.locator: Headword zùppa, pronunciation /ˈtsuppa/, and soup definition; entry directly read in independent audit 2026-10-01.
sources.whatItSupports: Independently corroborates initial voiceless /ts/ and geminate /p/ in zuppa. The entry /ˈtsuppa/ is normalized to /ˈtsupːa/ for the pack’s consonant-length convention.
sources.limitations: Entry text verified; no source recording auditioned. This source supports lexical pronunciation and meaning, not a training-effectiveness or stimulus-list claim.

sources.title: Peter Roach (2004), British English: Received Pronunciation
sources.locator: Journal of the International Phonetic Association 34(2), pp. 239–245; primary PDF read, consonant and vowel illustrations.

sources.limitations: Describes RP in 2004, not every contemporary Southern British speaker or the UK as a whole. It supplies no evidence that these editorial pools or cross-word matching outperform other tasks.

sources.title: Collins English Dictionary: room (British English variants)
sources.locator: British English headword, two listed pronunciations /ruːm, rʊm/; consulted 1 October 2026.
sources.whatItSupports: Room has competing GOOSE and FOOT dictionary variants, supporting its exclusion from the core.
sources.limitations: An exclusion rationale, not a pool word, stimulus record or claim about every British speaker.

sources.title: GOOSE-fronting in Received Pronunciation across time: A trend study (2023)
sources.locator: Phonetic-environment coding and discussion of velarized /l/; publisher full text consulted 1 October 2026.
sources.whatItSupports: The study treats following dark /l/ separately and reports inhibition of GOOSE-fronting there, supporting a separate pre-/l/ context group.
sources.limitations: A descriptive RP corpus study across decades, not a training experiment or proof that every contemporary speaker has the same realization.

sources.title: Okada (1991): Japanese — Illustrations of the IPA
sources.locator: JIPA 21(2), pp.94–96; vowel-length examples and conventions on p.95.
sources.whatItSupports: Tokyo-area sound inventory, length contrasts, predictable consonant variants, high-vowel devoicing and independent pitch accent.
sources.limitations: Descriptive illustration of one speaker, not learner-training evidence. Our IPA conventions normalize its older symbols and omit pitch labels. No recordings reused.

sources.title: Vance (2001): Japanese — Orthography and Basic Phonology
sources.locator: NINJAL-hosted two-page excerpt; consonant and vowel tables, moraic segments and accent.
sources.whatItSupports: All five vowels have quantity contrasts; moraic nasal realization is context dependent; ordinary Japanese distinguishes the selected consonant categories.
sources.limitations: Short descriptive sketch, not a study of the chosen words. Broad /ɴ/ below is a moraic-nasal placeholder, not a claim of invariant uvular articulation.

sources.title: Tokyo University of Foreign Studies: Long Vowels
sources.locator: Explanation, Long Vowels 2.2.1.
sources.whatItSupports: Pedagogical distinction between one- and two-mora vowels; usual long-vowel readings of kana ei/ou and the need to separate orthography from sound.
sources.limitations: General teaching description, not word-specific phonetic validation. Selected /eː,oː/ readings require later recording review; no blanket conversion of every ei/ou sequence.

sources.title: Tokyo University of Foreign Studies: k / g
sources.locator: Explanation, k / g 1.6.1.
sources.whatItSupports: Japanese /k–ɡ/ is an instructional priority for learners whose native laryngeal categories differ.
sources.limitations: Pedagogical motivation, not a controlled efficacy experiment; no ranking of all learner populations implied.

sources.title: Tokyo University of Foreign Studies: t / d
sources.locator: Explanation, t / d 1.5.1.
sources.whatItSupports: Japanese /t–d/ can be misidentified through different native-language laryngeal cues.
sources.limitations: Teaching guidance, not proof that these word pools or this training method are effective.

sources.title: Tokyo University of Foreign Studies: Consonant-glide
sources.locator: Explanation, Consonant-glide 1.11.1.
sources.whatItSupports: A contracted consonant-glide mora must not be expanded into an additional full /i/ syllable.
sources.limitations: Supports the moraic interpretation of contracted sounds; not an experiment on the particular /s–ɕ/ pool.

sources.title: Tsukada, Hirata & Roengpitya (2014): Cross-language perception of Japanese vowel length contrasts
sources.locator: PubMed abstract; JSLHR 57(3), 805–814; DOI 10.1044/2014_JSLHR-S-12-0416.
sources.whatItSupports: American English, Italian and Thai listeners were tested on Japanese vowel length with AXB discrimination.
sources.limitations: Abstract inspected; full stimulus list not recovered. Evidence concerns the length class, not every vowel-specific bank or training success. No word receives stimulus provenance from it.

sources.title: Tajima et al. (2008): Training English listeners to perceive phonemic length contrasts in Japanese
sources.locator: Full paper, JASA 123, 397–413; abstract and pp.398–400 on temporal context and training.
sources.whatItSupports: Vowel-length identification training and tests of rate, word position, presentation context and transfer. Results support treating those variables explicitly.
sources.limitations: Reported generalization was limited. Identification with feedback is not our cross-word audio-only ABX; the paper does not establish its superiority. No word-list membership imported here.

sources.title: Tsukada, Kim & Han (2020): Perception of Japanese consonant length by native speakers of Korean differing in Japanese learning experience
sources.locator: Interspeech 2020, pp.4471–4475; methods §2 and Table 1 on p.4472.
sources.whatItSupports: Korean learner groups completed /t,k/ length AXB trials with three different speakers per trial.
sources.limitations: Cross-sectional perception, not randomized training. X differed in speaker/token, not necessarily lexical word; this is not a validation of our cross-word design.

sources.title: Tsukada, Kim & Han (2020): Table 1, Japanese word stimuli
sources.locator: Table 1, p.4472, directly read in text and rendered PDF image.
sources.whatItSupports: Documents the exact selected readings/senses saka, kako, haka, sakka, kakko, oto, wata and otto. Three retained paired frames also share the table’s accent-type grouping.
sources.limitations: Only those eight matching lexical items receive this source in stimulusSourceIds. Hakka meaning mint is not our 発火 ignition. Remaining words are editorial dictionary additions; no audio permission inferred.

sources.title: Sadakata et al. (2014): Language specific listening of Japanese geminate consonants
sources.locator: Abstract and introduction; materials use pseudo words containing /ss/ and manipulated silence-plus-/s/.
sources.whatItSupports: Cross-language perception provides context for sustained-frication geminates.
sources.limitations: Does not directly test our real-word /s–sː/ comparison or training method. Pseudo words were not imported.
sources.license: Article CC BY; no recordings reused.

sources.title: Yamakawa, Amano & Kondo (2022): Perceptual boundary and discrimination sensitivity of Japanese singleton and geminate stops
sources.locator: Publisher abstract; Acoustical Science and Technology 43(2), 96–104.
sources.whatItSupports: Adjacent vowel devoicing and speaking rate affected stop-length perception in Japanese and Taiwanese Mandarin listeners.
sources.limitations: Abstract inspected; not certification of our lexical exemplars. No stimulus membership assigned.

reviewPolicy.countUnit: Distinct spellings within each sound category; repeated contexts and homograph senses do not increase depth. Broad IPA forms are counted separately: homophones do not add a new listening example, and context depth requires both counts to meet the floor.
reviewPolicy.claimLimit: An owner-set starting floor, not an experimentally established optimum or approval of any word, context or audio.

searchLog.outcome: Found primary 1991/1993 papers. Search-indexed methods were accessible; direct 1991 PMC page intermittently returned a browser challenge.

searchLog.outcome: Found 2008 follow-up and PubMed record; nine-vowel inventory supports category breadth, not these word lists.

searchLog.query: English dental fricatives theta s training Japanese Chinese identification stimuli appendix IRIS
searchLog.outcome: Found and read Lambacher et al. 2001 primary PDF, including Table 1 and context-dependent confusions.

searchLog.outcome: Found Giannakopoulou et al. 2017 Greek study, Table S1 link and OSF project https://osf.io/8anzk/. Supplement retrieval failed; no imported full list claimed.

searchLog.outcome: Located IRIS search service, but no matching downloadable stimulus record was verified in this pass.

searchLog.outcome: Read institutional UCL PDF; discrimination versus identification is not equivalent to a test of this product format.

searchLog.outcome: Recovered actual Table A1 in the full published-paper mirror. Publisher PDF endpoint redirected to a minimal page; DOI and bibliographic metadata matched.

searchLog.outcome: Read Saarland university inventory referencing Ladefoged and Wells; used for phonological categories, not training proof.

searchLog.outcome: Opened targeted publisher entries. Other new lookup URLs remain explicitly marked as unverified editorial references.

searchLog.outcome: Read primary Leong et al. 2018 methods and limitations; /ɛ–æ/ training, final /t–d/ generalization, initial /t–d/ ceiling.

searchLog.query: Cebrian Gavaldà Gorba Carlet differential effects identification discrimination L2 vowel 2024
searchLog.outcome: Read publisher abstract and methods following root-agent source discovery. Appendix A image requests returned cache misses; retained as contrast/task evidence only.

searchLog.query: Targeted independent publisher checks: thimble/symbol, thrill/frill, berry/belly, grass/glass, mouth noun, path; American cat/cot, cap/cop, lack/lock
searchLog.outcome: Selected dictionary IPA and senses confirmed. Plural -z and /r/→/ɹ/ notation in berries/bellies remain explicit editorial adaptations. Selected /æ/ maintained for American grass/glass/path; alternatives are not mixed.

searchLog.query: Suemitsu et al. 2026 10.3389/fnhum.2026.1743034 methods and supplemental stimulus table
searchLog.outcome: Root supplied primary paper; full text §2.3.2 read. Body documents cat–cot; supplement link points to page anchor without returning a table in this pass. Added a three-frame American TRAP/LOT draft, with documented and curated words distinguished.

searchLog.outcome: Applied parent-agent overlap exclusions to one English vowel pool, removed its affected pair and unused dictionary references, and retained fourteen entries per category. No replacement vocabulary was added; reserved words are not enumerated here.

gaps: Text-only draft for owner/native review. No audio generated, approved or evaluated.
Common-word status is an editorial suitability screen, not a measured frequency threshold. Historically integrated ordinary words retained; etymology alone is not exclusion.
Every contrast has at least four spellings per side and one context with four per side. Smaller secondary groups remain; homophones do not imply acoustic diversity.
Inherited dictionary sources include lookup targets not all freshly opened. New entries were directly checked; this is not full independent certification of every inherited word.
French /ø–œ/ common-word coverage retains strong coda/dialect cues. Do not present these pools as a coda-controlled minimal-pair assessment.
French /ɲ/ may surface [nj]; mid vowels and jeûne/jeune vary regionally. Selected /a–ɑ/ merger explains tasse/vase normalization. Do not silently change dialect.

English reference varieties are explicit General American and Standard Southern British. SSBE now has 22 selected comparisons in its separate bank; no country-wide accent or full British coverage claimed.
German schwa/rhotic normalization explicit. Löffel normalized from /ˈlœfl/ to /ˈlœfəl/. Existing spulen exact-IPA gap remains.

Backlog requiring further primary L2 evidence and pools: English /tʃ–dʒ/, FACE/DRESS, GOAT/LOT, stress/clusters; German stop voicing/aspiration, /f–v/, affricates/diphthongs; French oral /ɔ/ versus nasal /ɔ̃/, glides/liaison/schwa. Not universally difficult contrasts.
New /θ–t/ and /ɛ–ɛ̃/ entries are inventory candidates, not inspected L2 stimuli. No new word gains a stimulusSourceId. No ABX-superiority claim.
Retained documented stimulus provenance preserved; vocabulary removed from practice remains in its historical source, not in these pools.

gaps: This is an ordinary-vocabulary and depth audit of the current 35 Spanish/Italian/Portuguese contrasts, not an exhaustive inventory of Spanish, Italian or Portuguese phonology or every learner-L1 difficulty.
At least four distinct spellings in a shared context is a curriculum-depth rule, not a research-derived efficacy threshold. New editorial dictionary words are not documented experimental stimuli.
Spanish final-o vowel subgroups remain at three per side; final-a groups reach four. The two-syllable stress contrast is explicitly prosodic.

Portuguese final-stressed /o–ɔ/ and the inherited unmatched nasal-vowel study subgroup remain too small for cross-word trials. Their independently sufficient first-stressed / before-t groups must be selected instead.

Italian broader affricate and fricative inventories, Portuguese remaining nasal-vowel qualities and palatal contrasts, and Spanish additional dialect-specific contrasts require separate literature and lexical review; no exhaustive coverage is claimed.

No new recordings were generated or auditioned. Standard Italian regional vowel variation, Brazilian strong-r/affrication/final-vowel variation, and Spanish intervocalic approximants need explicit voice and recording review.
Primary dictionary evidence supports lexical form and sense, not numerical corpus frequency. Ordinary-usage selection here is editorial and remains open to owner/native-speaker review.

Martinez, Goad & Dow specifically motivate future /e–ẽ/ and /i–ĩ/ review. The current /a–ɐ̃/ pool is not a substitute for those distinct contrasts; no dictionary word pool for them was added during this bounded audit.
This is a research overlay with full replacements, not a live curriculum change. All entries remain draft and require owner text review before audio.

All 24 Russian/Mandarin comparisons have at least one declared compatible group with at least four distinct spellings per category. Four Russian comparisons and Mandarin s/sh have four per side; other pools have five.

Russian initial/medial palatalization material is deferred rather than pooled with final targets. This sacrifices position coverage to establish sufficient compatible depth; more controlled groups can be researched later.
Russian /ɨ i/ remains a coupled consonant-plus-vowel comparison. Its score cannot isolate vowel learning from onset palatalization.

Russian coverage remains non-exhaustive: /ʂ ɕː/, /ts tɕ/, further palatalization pairs, unstressed reduction, and additional voicing/place contrasts need separately sourced word pools and learner-priority evidence.

Mandarin coverage remains non-exhaustive: dental/retroflex/alveolopalatal affricates and fricatives, /i y u/, other vowel distinctions, non-low-vowel nasal rhymes, neutral tone and connected-speech sandhi remain separate research gaps.
The nasal pool intentionally keeps low-vowel rhymes separate and marks vowel coarticulation. A pure isolated-coda learning claim would require a different validated design.

Primary dictionary facts were inspected mainly through indexed text, not a certified lexicographic audit. Taiwan lexical readings do not certify Putonghua phonetics. No dictionaries or studies provide pronunciation approval for future TTS.
No newly added word is labelled as a study stimulus. Any retained stimulusSourceIds were inherited only for an exact matching word and IPA from a previously checked study target.

gaps: This is a bounded reference bank, not exhaustive coverage of Southern British phonology or learner-specific difficulty. Learner-L1 priorities and optimal task allocation require further evidence.

FACE, PRICE, CHOICE, MOUTH and GOAT contrasts; BATH/PALM; NEAR/SQUARE/CURE; weak vowels, connected speech and additional consonant positions remain outside this expansion. Do not manufacture counterparts for merged or unstable categories.
FOOT/GOOSE has a five-per-side pre-obstruent core and a separate two-per-side pre-/l/ group. The latter does not meet the owner’s four-per-side context floor.
No audio was generated or validated. Labels and lexical pools do not establish native naturalness, precise vowel quality, within-category voice compatibility or task efficacy.

The two earlier British units were moved here unchanged during canonical integration. Their existing reference sources remain globally available from the English research pack; source IDs and review identities are preserved.

gaps: Text-only draft. No audio generated, selected, auditioned or approved. Counts describe lexical candidates, not launch-ready lessons.

This bounded first bank is not an exhaustive inventory. /a–aː/ is deferred because this pass did not establish five ordinary independent long-a lexemes in one useful context under the current vocabulary constraints; this is not a claim that such vocabulary is impossible.

Singleton/geminate /p/ is deferred: common native/Sino-Japanese singleton examples tend to introduce a postnasal context, while geminates are medial elsewhere. A future pack may use carefully selected established loans or another controlled design instead of quietly mixing contexts.

Pitch accent is an independent lexical dimension and is not a target here. No Tokyo accent dictionary was imported; exact accent patterns remain to be reviewed before audio/trial balancing. The three listed minimal pairs are segmentally matched and share accent-type cells in Tsukada Table 1, not a declaration that every natural token has identical F0.
Moraic-nasal presence/length, palatalized versus full-i sequences, /ɕ–tɕ/, vowel quality comparisons, additional voicing categories and position-specific expansions remain outside this first scope.

Four vowel-specific banks are labeled phonology: L2 studies motivate quantity generally, but exact vowel-specific stimulus lists were not inspected for these words. The /s–sː/ bank is also phonology, with related pseudo-word research clearly qualified.

Broad target-position groups are not complete acoustic matching. Word length, segmental neighbors, accent, vowel devoicing and speaking rate need checks during the later recording discussion; no fixed duration threshold is endorsed.
